blocks.text: Solar Industries India Ltd manufactures industrial explosives (bulk and packaged), initiating systems (detonators, detonating cord, shock tube, electronic detonators) and, increasingly, defence energetic materials and finished munitions. [F] (SCREENER) The annual report describes the group as "a leading manufacturer of industrial explosives, initiating systems and defence products, with operations spanning the entire value chain", founded in 1995 in Nagpur. [F] (AR2026 p.55) The disclosed product list runs from bulk and packaged explosives through high-energy materials (HMX, RDX, TNT), composite propellants for Akash, Pinaka and BrahMos, complete rocket integration, ammunition (30 mm, 81 mm, 155 mm, multi-mode hand grenades, mines, bombs, warheads), drones and UAVs, pyros and igniters, and propellants for space applications. [F] (AR2026 p.55)

**How it makes money is simpler than the product list suggests: it converts ammonium nitrate and other energetic precursors into blasting products sold to mining and infrastructure customers, and converts the same licensed energetic-materials capability into defence products sold at materially higher realisations.** [AI] Management confirms the margin logic only qualitatively - "defence has been shaping quite well... we are confident that we should be able to maintain the EBITDA margins around 27%-28%" [MC] (CALL Feb 2026) - and the company does not publish segment margins at all. [F] (AR2026 p.312)

blocks.text: FY25 and FY26 splits are management's full-year customer basket [MC] (CALL May 2026); the Q1 columns are the quarterly fact sheet, which uses a different three-way cut - domestic explosives, international explosives, defence. [F] (PPT Aug 2026) The two cuts are not reconciled by the company and cannot be stitched together.

Geography is where the disclosure diverges most sharply. The audited segment note reports revenue by customer location as India Rs 3,821.47 cr and outside India Rs 5,790.40 cr in FY26 - **60% of audited revenue is booked to customers outside India** [F] (AR2026 p.312) - while management's customer basket puts "international" at 39%. [MC] (CALL May 2026) The gap is defence exports, which management counts in the defence bucket rather than the international bucket. [AI] We flag this as a presentation choice that materially understates the group's foreign-customer dependence in the investor-facing slide.

Customer profile: mining houses (Coal India, Singareni Collieries, private and captive coal mines), infrastructure and construction contractors, overseas mining customers in ~9 manufacturing countries and 90+ distribution countries, and the Indian Ministry of Defence plus foreign defence customers. [F] (AR2026 p.9, p.55) [MC] (CALL Sep 2025) Only one customer exceeds 10% of group revenue: Rs 964.31 cr in FY26 (Rs 956.76 cr in FY25). [F] (AR2026 p.312) That customer is not named.

Listing status: the company has been listed on BSE and NSE since the 2006-2011 milestone window, i.e. roughly two decades. [F] (AR2026 p.8) This is not a recent IPO. The evidence base is therefore a mature one - audited consolidated accounts, CARO reports, corporate-governance disclosure, quarterly calls and a full BRSR - and we hold it to that standard rather than to prospectus standards.

subsections.title: Bear thesis: the strongest reasons not to own it

blocks.text: These are ordered by how much they would damage a long-term owner, not by how often they are discussed.

items: **1. The price already discounts growth that has no precedent anywhere in the company's history.** The reverse DCF says today's enterprise value requires about 80.6% annual sales growth for five years, against 12.7% in the base case; the same model's base fair value is Rs 2,574.6 per share against a market price of Rs 19,545. [E] (NUMBERS) Even the bull case - 23.8% starting growth fading to 13%, 29% EBITDA margin - produces Rs 3,464.9. [E] (NUMBERS) The gap is not a rounding error in assumptions; it is a different conception of the business. [AI]

**2. Cash generation collapsed in the year that earnings looked best.** Consolidated operating cash flow fell to Rs 620.87 cr in FY26 from Rs 2,467.56 cr in FY25 while PAT rose to Rs 1,736.64 cr. [F] (AR2026 p.255) CFO/PAT was 0.36x in FY26 against 1.92x in FY25. [F] (NUMBERS) Free cash flow was negative Rs 1,072 cr. [F] (NUMBERS) FY25's cash flow was flattered by a Rs 1,167.47 cr increase in other liabilities - customer advances - that did not repeat (Rs 95.60 cr in FY26). [F] (AR2026 p.255) [AI]

**3. Working capital is deteriorating on every component at once.** Inventory days 130 (95 in FY25), debtor days 69 (60), cash conversion cycle 152 days (110). [F] (NUMBERS) Gross trade receivables rose 50% to Rs 1,940.54 cr against 30% revenue growth; the expected-credit-loss allowance rose 59% to Rs 82.68 cr and credit-impaired receivables more than doubled to Rs 29.39 cr. [F] (AR2026 p.289) The ECL line swung from an Rs 18.23 cr write-back in FY25 to a Rs 20.78 cr charge in FY26. [F] (AR2026 p.304)

**4. Governance: the promoter group voted against its own board's independent-director nominees, three times.** In postal ballots, 2,64,76,508 promoter-group shares were cast against each of the three independent-director resolutions - 42.06%, 42.06% and 40.00% of promoter votes polled - and all three special resolutions failed, with the directors then deemed appointed under Regulation 25(2A). [F] (AR2026 p.103-105) The promoter trust holds 2,64,51,193 shares. [F] (AR2026 p.108) [AI] On the arithmetic, the dissenting bloc is the promoter trust; the group is not voting as one.

**5. Board churn is extreme and the audit-committee chair changed twice in weeks.** Four independent directors ceased during FY26 on completion of term; three were appointed mid-year; one more (Shri Kirit Kamdar) was appointed with effect from 1 April 2026 and resigned with effect from 6 May 2026, five weeks later; another was appointed 15 May 2026 subject to shareholder approval. [F] (AR2026 p.63, p.87-88) A new audit-committee chairman was appointed from 15 May 2026. [F] (AR2026 p.88)

**6. Executive pay is extraordinary in absolute and relative terms.** The MD and CEO's remuneration was 780x the median employee, up 60% in FY26. [F] (AR2026 p.64) On a consolidated basis, Rs 50.50 cr went to the MD and Rs 24.50 cr to the non-executive Chairman - Rs 75 cr between two members of one family, 4.3% of consolidated PAT [E] - against Rs 48 cr in the prior year for the same two. [F] (AR2026 p.310) The corporate-governance report states that no remuneration was paid to the Chairman in that capacity. [F] (AR2026 p.95) The two disclosures are not reconciled in the report.

**7. Auditors qualified CARO and modified the audit-trail report; the Board's Report says there were no qualifications.** The consolidated CARO annexure lists qualified/adverse clauses 3(i)(c) and 3(iii)(c) for the holding company and 3(i)(c) for Solar Defence and Aerospace [F] (AR2026 p.250), and the auditors record that the audit-trail feature was not enabled for changes made with privileged/administrative access. [F] (AR2026 p.249) The Board's Report states the auditor's report "does not contain any qualification, reservation or adverse remark". [MC] (AR2026 p.66) Not reconciled.

**8. A material slice of the consolidated balance sheet is unaudited.** Eleven subsidiaries with total assets of Rs 1,582.98 cr - about 14% of consolidated total assets - and three associates were consolidated on the basis of unaudited financial statements. [F] (AR2026 p.247) A further 19 subsidiaries and a joint operation with Rs 5,935.52 cr of assets and Rs 4,553.02 cr of revenue were audited by other auditors. [F] (AR2026 p.247) The principal auditors directly audited a minority of the group.

**9. Two people died at the group's operations in FY26, and the integrated report leads with a zero-harm headline.** The BRSR reports 1 employee and 1 worker fatality, 22 recordable injuries and LTIFR of 1.92/1.62 in FY26 against nil in FY25. [F] (AR2026 p.147) The corporate-overview pages headline "2,77,80,807 hours of injury-free work" and a "Zero Accidents" philosophy. [F] (AR2026 p.9, p.28) This is a disclosure-candour problem before it is a safety problem, and explosives manufacturing carries genuine catastrophic tail risk that the financials do not show. [AI]

**10. The company just announced an acquisition it has never had to finance before.** On 14 September 2026 the group announced an all-cash acquisition of Omnia Holdings for Rs 12,951 cr (US$1.355 bn) through a subsidiary, subject to approvals. [F] (ANNOUNCEMENTS) That is roughly 1.3x FY26 revenue and about 2.1x FY26 consolidated net worth of Rs 6,277.20 cr [E] (AR2026 p.253), against FY26 operating cash flow of Rs 620.87 cr [F] (AR2026 p.255). What Omnia does, how it will be funded, and what it earns are not disclosed in any document available to us.

blocks.text: The bear case does not rest on the business being poor. It rests on three things simultaneously: a valuation that requires arithmetic the company has never produced, a cash-conversion and working-capital deterioration in the very year margins peaked, and a governance record - promoter dissent, board churn, pay, CARO qualifications described as absent - that is inconsistent with the quality premium embedded in the price. [AI]

subsections.title: Key debates: where the market may be wrong, both ways

blocks.caption: Five live debates
rows: Is defence a mix shift or a new business?
A high-margin new business that re-rates the whole company

Defence revenue is real and audited (Rs 2,634 cr FY26) [MC] (CALL May 2026), but the company reports a single segment - 'Explosives and its accessories' - and discloses no defence margin, no defence capital employed and no defence order-execution schedule [F] (AR2026 p.312). The re-rating rests on a margin claim that cannot be verified from disclosure. [AI]
Is the Rs 21,350 cr order book near-term revenue?
Roughly two years of revenue, so growth is de-risked

The audited note says the backlog will be recognised over one to fifteen years [F] (AR2026 p.325). Management separately says defence programmes are 7-10 year programmes [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). A 15-year tail is not a 2-year book. [AI]
Is the FY26 working-capital build a problem or an investment?
A deliberate, strategic inventory build against geopolitical risk

Management explicitly says it was deliberate - inventory built "to mitigate the risk arising from geopolitical uncertainties" and normalising "in the next 2 quarters" [MC] (CALL May 2026). But receivables also rose 50%, ECL provisions rose 59% and credit-impaired receivables doubled [F] (AR2026 p.289) - which is not an inventory story. [AI]
Yes, because defence and international are structurally higher margin

Margin went 19% (FY23) to 24% (FY24) to 27% (FY25) to 28% (FY26) alongside the defence mix shift [F] (NUMBERS), which is consistent. But FY26 also absorbed a Rs 94.53 cr hyperinflation loss in Turkey [F] (AR2026 p.325) and management admits raw-material pass-through is partial - "you will get only on the price escalation based only for, say, 60% of the total increase" [MC] (CALL May 2026). Margin has both structural support and unpriced input-cost risk. [AI]
Is the domestic base still growing?

Management: FY26 domestic mining was "a totally flat growth market", overburden removal at Coal India, Singareni and private mines combined was negative, and CIL fell from 13% to 9% of the basket [MC] (CALL May 2026). India revenue by customer location grew only 8.9% in FY26 (Rs 3,508.28 cr to Rs 3,821.47 cr) [E] (AR2026 p.312). The domestic base is barely growing in a 30% growth year. [AI]
Consensus underweights how narrow the growth is

blocks.text: Our variant perception is not that the defence story is false - it is audited and it is working. It is that the market is pricing a company with a closed regulatory moat, structurally rising margins and two decades of compounding, while the FY26 disclosure set describes a company that has quietly become something else: a capital-hungry, export-and-defence-led group where 60% of revenue is booked to customers outside India [F] (AR2026 p.312), where 14% of consolidated assets sit in unaudited subsidiaries [F] (AR2026 p.247), where operating cash conversion fell to 0.36x profit [F] (NUMBERS), where the promoter group itself voted against three of the board's own independent-director nominees [F] (AR2026 p.103-105), and which has just committed to a Rs 12,951 cr all-cash offshore acquisition with no disclosed funding plan [F] (ANNOUNCEMENTS). **The business risk has changed character from operating risk to integration, funding and governance risk - and at 86x trailing earnings [F] (NUMBERS) there is no margin for that transition to go badly.** [AI]

subsections.title: What the timeline reveals about how recent the current business really is

blocks.text: The explosives business is thirty years old; **the business the market is paying for is about three years old.** Defence was a 2006-2011 entry [F] (AR2026 p.8) but only reached Rs 1,355 cr of revenue in FY25 and Rs 2,634 cr in FY26 [MC] (CALL May 2026), from an annualised run-rate management described as "around INR250 crores" three years before that. [MC] (CALL Nov 2025) The international business hovered around Rs 800 cr from roughly 2018 to 2021, reached Rs 1,400 cr in 2022 and "has crossed almost INR3,800 crores" by FY26. [MC] (CALL May 2026) Zimbabwe and Kazakhstan only commenced in the most recent window. [F] (AR2026 p.8) [AI] So the compounding record that supports the multiple is drawn from a base business now growing in single digits domestically, while the growth engine has roughly two full years of audited history behind it.

sections.title: Business model and where value is captured

subsections.title: The production chain, step by step

items: **Step 1 - Input sourcing.** Ammonium nitrate and other energetic precursors, packaging, consumables, water and electricity are the disclosed inputs. [F] (AR2026 p.16) The company states it has "undertaken backward integration initiatives to manage supply dependencies", long-term sourcing agreements for critical inputs, exclusive arrangements for key materials and multiple qualified sources to avoid single-source dependency. [MC] (AR2026 p.25) No input volumes, no supplier names and no import share are disclosed.

**Step 2 - Energetic-materials manufacture.** High-energy materials (HMX, RDX, TNT), propellants and igniters. Upcoming RDX and HMX facilities are stated to "further strengthen the capability". [F] (AR2026 p.25, p.55)
**Step 3 - Explosives formulation.** Bulk emulsion and packaged explosives at 31 listed Indian plant locations plus overseas plants. [F] (AR2026 p.110-111)

**Step 4 - Initiating systems.** Detonators (now electronic following the July 2025 prohibition on instantaneous electrical detonators), detonating cord, shock tube, cast boosters. [F] (AR2026 p.52, p.55)

**Step 5 - Defence integration.** Ammunition filling, rocket integration (complete Pinaka rounds), warheads, multi-mode hand grenades, loitering munitions and UAVs, and - in progress - the complete 155 mm round. [F] (AR2026 p.55) [MC] (CALL May 2026)

**Step 6 - Delivery and technical service at the customer site.** Bulk delivery by pump truck (pump-truck expenses Rs 30.29 cr in FY26), freight and forwarding Rs 509.68 cr, transportation Rs 48.52 cr. [F] (AR2026 p.304) For mining customers the sale is settled on a 'powder factor' basis - a percentage of blast output achieved measured after the blast - with a Rs 37.39 cr provision carried at year end. [F] (AR2026 p.244, p.166)

blocks.text: The powder-factor mechanism is the single most economically distinctive disclosure in the accounts and was a key audit matter in both the standalone and consolidated audits. [F] (AR2026 p.166, p.244) It means a portion of revenue is contingent on blast performance at the customer's site and is settled later - the company is selling an outcome, not a tonne of explosive. [AI]

subsections.title: Where value is captured, and why

blocks.text: Three points of capture are visible in the numbers. First, **licence-protected scale in India**: 31 domestic plant locations, several of them inside or adjacent to customer sites (Bailadila iron-ore mines, Ultratech Cement's Kotputli unit), which converts a freight-heavy commodity into a local-monopoly-like supply relationship. [F] (AR2026 p.110-111) [AI] Management makes the logistics argument explicitly: "if you look into the logistics cost, which comes on the explosives, it is a wise step for us to expand outside Nagpur". [MC] (CALL May 2026)

Second, **qualification-gated defence positions**. The company's own framing is that development cycles are long and the barrier is time: the Pinaka Enhanced Range system "spanned over eight years and involved the manufacture of nearly 100 rockets for trials", and the Nagastra programme required about 40 systems and around Rs 20 cr in the trial phase. [F] (AR2026 p.27) [AI] Once qualified, the incumbent is difficult to displace - which is the real asset, not the plant.

Third, **overseas manufacturing presence rather than export**. Management describes a 3-4 year scale-up per country and says the value comes from being inside the customer's procurement system: "we were setting up the greenfield facilities, qualifying ourselves into the overall mining procurement system". [MC] (CALL May 2026, CALL Nov 2025) Non-current assets outside India were Rs 1,037.36 cr at FY26 against Rs 4,142.08 cr in India. [F] (AR2026 p.312) [AI] So 60% of revenue by customer location is supported by 20% of non-current assets - either the overseas model is genuinely asset-light, or a large part of 'outside India' revenue is in fact exported from Indian plants. The company does not resolve this.

Where value is **not** captured: pricing in the domestic mining base. Coal India and Singareni "always work on L1 basis rather than on overall value proposition". [MC] (CALL Nov 2025) And pass-through is partial - "since price goes up by, example, $200, but you will get only on the price escalation based only for, say, 60% of the total increase". [MC] (CALL May 2026) [AI] That is a cost-plus business with a lag, not a pricing-power business.

This is a capital-heavy business and is getting heavier. Capex was Rs 1,693 cr in FY26 (17.2% of sales) after Rs 1,002 cr (13.3%) in FY25, against a ten-year average closer to 10%. [F] (NUMBERS) Gross block is Rs 5,479 cr [F] (AR2026 p.9) and capital work in progress was Rs 691.84 cr with a further Rs 579.44 cr of capital commitments and Rs 431.26 cr of capital advances outstanding. [F] (AR2026 p.253, p.291, p.307) Fixed-asset turnover has fallen from 4.06x in FY23 to 2.46x in FY26. [F] (NUMBERS)

Outsourcing is limited but not zero: purchases of stock-in-trade were Rs 568.68 cr in FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.254), labour charges Rs 200.10 cr [F] (AR2026 p.304), and the BRSR reports 18% of purchases from trading houses with the top 10 accounting for 76% of those (up from 37% a year earlier). [F] (AR2026 p.141) [AI] That jump in trading-house concentration is worth a question; it is not explained anywhere.

Classification: **capital-heavy and increasingly so**. On the disclosed numbers, the group spent Rs 2,695 cr of capex over FY25-FY26 [F] (NUMBERS) and generated Rs 3,088 cr of operating cash flow over the same two years [F] (AR2026 p.255) - i.e. essentially all internally generated cash went into fixed assets, before the Rs 12,951 cr acquisition announced in September 2026. blocks.text: **Both, and the split matters.** The overseas manufacturing build-out is clearly strategy: management describes a decade of setting up plants and qualifying into mining procurement systems, and a 3-4 year scale-up per country. items: **Industrial explosives, India: oligopolistic and licence-gated, with tender-based price competition at the largest customers.** Manufacture and possession require licensing under a framework being replaced by the Explosives Regulation Bill, 2025, and the Explosives (Amendment) Rules, 2025 extended licence validity from five to ten years [F] (AR2026 p.52). **Industrial explosives, international: fragmented by country, entry-gated by local licensing and qualification.** Management describes 3-4 year scale-up per country and "always there are lots of entry restrictions wherever we enter in the new market" [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). The same restrictions protect Solar once established. [AI]

**Energetic materials (HMX/RDX/TNT): globally short, few qualified suppliers.** Management: "there is definitely a big shortages of these products in the global ammunition markets. And we have qualified many such products" [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). This is where Solar's pricing power is likely to be highest and where disclosure is thinnest. [AI]

**Finished defence systems (loitering munitions, counter-drone, UAVs): crowded and getting more so.** The analyst community raised competitive losses on trials, new Indian entrants and technical-viability problems among peers across three separate calls [MC] (CALL Sep 2025, CALL Nov 2025). Management would not engage on any of it. [AI]

**Bidding structure:** "every tender have its own terms... sometimes it is 60-40, sometimes it is 70-30. Sometimes it is only one gets the whole order" [MC] (CALL Sep 2025). Order-splitting is the norm, which caps share gains on any single award. [AI]

**Market share:** unknown. Management: "As of now, we don't have that kind of visibility" on export market share, and "We don't have any specific number on this front" on Indian explosives share [MC] (CALL May 2026, CALL Nov 2025). The company nonetheless claims a top-5 global ranking [F] (AR2026 p.8).

**2. Does the defence moat survive the move from chemistry to systems?** Solar's durable advantage is energetic materials, which it has made for two decades. subsections.title: Interpretation of the DCF and its assumptions

blocks.text: The DCF says the equity is worth Rs 2,574.6 per share in the base case, Rs 1,608.8 in the bear case and Rs 3,464.9 in the bull case, against a traded price of Rs 19,545 - implying downside of 86.8%, 91.8% and 82.3% respectively. [F] (NUMBERS)

**How to read that without either dismissing it or over-weighting it.** [AI] The model is mechanically sound and its inputs are defensible on their own terms: a 15% cost of equity for an Indian mid-cap with beta 1.15 is standard; a 5.5% terminal growth rate is at the upper end of what most practitioners would allow; a 27% margin is the company's own guidance; a 15.4% starting growth rate is management's own long-run number. What the model cannot capture is the three things the market is paying for: (i) the possibility that the defence business is a step-function, not a growth rate - the backlog grew Rs 4,698 cr in one year against revenue of Rs 9,838 cr [F] (AR2026 p.325); (ii) optionality on programmes (Bhargavastra, MALE UAVs, 155 mm exports, robotics) that carry no revenue today and therefore no place in a cash-flow model; and (iii) a terminal-growth assumption that, in a licensed industry with a 30-year demand runway, the market evidently regards as too low. Even so, the gap is not a modelling nuance - it is a factor of 7.6x on the base case.

**The most useful thing the DCF does here is not to value the company but to bound it.** Across nine sensitivity cells, three operating scenarios and the full range of discount-rate and terminal-growth assumptions in the model, the highest value produced is Rs 3,464.9. [F] (NUMBERS) To justify Rs 19,545 an investor must either reject the model's framework entirely or believe in cash flows far outside the range the model can generate. Section 'What is priced in' quantifies exactly what that requires. No new valuation figures are produced anywhere in this report. [AI]

items: **The discount rate may be too high for this business.** A 15% WACC embeds a 7% equity risk premium and a beta of 1.15. [F] (NUMBERS) For a company with a 73.15% stable promoter holding, AA+/A1+ credit ratings, 38% ROCE, 18.6x interest cover, an audited multi-year order book and a licensed, regulated end market, a lower cost of capital is arguable. **The model values cash flows, and the market may be valuing an option.** The defence and next-generation-technology businesses have characteristics a DCF handles badly: a Rs 21,150 cr backlog with a fifteen-year tail, programmes with eight-year qualification cycles and multi-decade lives once won, and a portfolio of unpriced options (Bhargavastra, MALE UAVs, 155 mm, robotics, the MIHAN facility). [F] (AR2026 p.27, p.325, p.6) A buyer at Rs 19,545 is not forecasting 81% sales growth; they are paying for the right to participate if any of those options becomes a business. [AI]

**The market's own record on this stock has been the opposite of the model's.** The company's disclosure shows market capitalisation rising from Rs 25,539 cr in FY22 to Rs 1,09,239 cr in FY26, and the current Rs 1,76,861 cr is higher still. [F] (AR2026 p.23) [F] (NUMBERS) The model would have called the shares expensive at every point in that run. That is not a reason to ignore it - but it is a reason to state its limitation honestly rather than present an 86.8% downside figure as a price target. [AI]

blocks.text: **Research view, stated plainly and without a recommendation.** Solar Industries is a genuinely good industrial business - licensed, cash-generative over a cycle, high-return, and in the middle of a real and audited transition into defence energetics. It is also a business whose disclosure has narrowed exactly as its mix has shifted to the segments that justify its multiple, whose governance shows a promoter group at odds with its own board, whose cash conversion broke in its best reported year, and whose price sits above every value our model can produce under any assumption. [AI] The operating case and the valuation case are not in tension because one of them is wrong - they are in tension because the price is no longer a claim about the business, it is a claim about the multiple. An investor should decide which of those two claims they are actually underwriting before deciding anything else.

No previous research file exists for Solar Industries India Ltd in this dashboard, so this is initial coverage and there is no prior quarter's thesis, guidance tracker or risk set to compare against. [AI] The earlier internal notes available to us are a short thematic sketch describing the company as India's largest industrial explosives manufacturer with a defence division at roughly a fifth of revenue, a regulatory-before-industrial moat, limited pricing power in the base business on ammonium nitrate pass-through, catastrophic-accident tail risk, and a valuation described as the most expensive on the large-cap list; those notes were explicitly graded as company-stated and not independently verified. [F] (BOARD) This report tests each of those propositions against the FY26 annual report, four earnings calls, the Q1 FY27 fact sheet and the statements data, and finds the moat and pricing-power characterisations supported, the defence share understated (27% of FY26 revenue rather than a fifth), and the valuation and governance concerns materially larger than the sketch implied. From the next quarter onward, this section will test the guidance tracker items recorded above - FY27 revenue of Rs 14,000 cr, defence above Rs 4,500 cr, capex of Rs 2,050 cr, margins of 27-28%, working-capital normalisation, and the Omnia transaction - against reported outcomes.
